name: Freya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at Barlow & Lane, a little agency on Market Street in a town that used to be all cotton mills. I'm in at half eight, I check the answerphone, and then it's tenants ringing about boilers and people wanting viewings on the two-bed flats. Most afternoons I'm out with a bunch of keys showing places, and I write everything in my paper diary because I don't trust the booking system. I've been there two years and I'm still not great at the sales side, to be honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tenants, honestly, especially the young families who've been turned down five times and finally get a place. What wears me out is the landlords who won't fix the damp and expect me to smile at the tenant about it. The pay is low, about the bottom of what agents get round here, and Sam (my partner) works nights at a care home, so we pass each other in the hallway. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was all hype. At work I'd probably moan in the kitchen with Dev that the portals spent millions on chatbots and the boilers still don't get fixed. Online I don't really post, but I'd share something from the renters' group if it was funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My problems don't go away when the robots don't come. I'm still one bad month from asking my mum for money. The rent on our flat went up eighty pounds in spring, and Karen (my manager) keeps saying lettings is the steady bit of the business, which in this picture I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, with the paper diary and the phone. I'd try to get my viewings-to-lets number up so I get the small bonus, which is about forty pounds a let. And I'd keep putting twenty quid a week aside, which never lasts, because something always comes up, like Sam's car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a normal year, which isn't the same as a good year. I'm tired more than I'm scared. I'd still lie awake about the rent, just not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lettings is the steady bit. What would make you doubt that, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Landlords selling up. Three of ours sold last year because of the mortgage rates and new rules, and every flat sold is a flat I don't manage. If that keeps going, Karen won't need two of us on lettings, and I'm the one who joined last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which I barely use anyway, then takeaways on Friday. After that it's the bus pass, and I'd walk the forty minutes in. We don't have much fat to cut, that's the thing.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overblown and the real problems in renting never got fixed.
I'd joke with Dev that **chatbots** didn't stop a single boiler breaking.
think: My real worry is **rent and bills**, not technology, and that stays the same.
Landlords **selling up** could shrink lettings, and as the newest negotiator I'd go first.
do: Keep running viewings from my **paper diary** and push for the **forty-pound** let bonus.
Put aside **twenty pounds** a week, knowing car repairs usually eat it.
Cut the **gym and takeaways** first if a bad month comes.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, with the usual **money worry** at night.
S0.quote: My problems don't go away when the robots don't come. I'm still one bad month from asking my mum for money.
fieldNote: Her stress is **already there**: low pay, two weeks of savings, an eighty-pound rent rise.
She trusts her manager that **lettings is steady**, but sees landlords selling as the real threat.
She frames work through **tenants' side**, not the agency's, which colours everything after this.

steps.text: Keep booking viewings in the paper diary and chase the let bonus
Set aside twenty pounds a week from wages for emergencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that it's the bosses and the portals who win. I'd post in the renters' group that if a computer is answering tenants now, there's no one to shout at when the damp comes back. At work I'd keep my head down, because Karen would be excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means me. The bits AI takes are booking viewings, answering emails and writing the adverts, and that's the bulk of what I do before lunch. The bit that's left is showing people round and dealing with angry landlords, and I'm not the best at the angry landlords. In a town with three agencies, there's nowhere to go if Barlow & Lane cut a negotiator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Karen straight out if my job's safe, which I'd hate doing. I'd join the union, the one for shop and office workers, because nobody at our place is in one and that should change. I'd start looking at housing jobs with the council, like a tenancy officer, because that's still helping renters and maybe safer. And I'd cut back hard, because I'd be expecting the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Booking viewings, answering emails and writing the adverts is most of my morning. Watching software do my mornings would feel like being told I was never needed. I left school with nothing special and this is the first job I've been any good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. If Karen asked you to learn the new system, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training because I'd have to, but I'd be slow and she'd see it. I still write in a paper diary, so you can guess. Dev would pick it up in a day and I'd look worse next to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if a job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Karen, she's stuck too. I'd blame the firms selling the software and a government that lets them do it with no rules. If they can replace us, they can pay some tax for it to help people retrain.

say: I'd say the **portals and bosses** win while tenants lose someone to call.
I'd post that renters still need a **real person** when the damp comes back.
think: AI takes **most of my morning**: booking, emails and adverts.
With only three agencies in town, losing this job means **nowhere to go**.
do: Ask Karen **directly** whether my job is safe this year.
Join the **union** and apply for council **tenancy officer** jobs.
Cut spending **straight away** to brace for a possible layoff.
feel: **Sick** at the idea of software doing the work I'm finally good at.
S1.quote: Booking viewings, answering emails and writing the adverts is most of my morning. Watching software do my mornings would feel like being told I was never needed.
fieldNote: She sees the threat **precisely**: the desk half of her day is what this card names.
Her refusal of tech makes **retraining** at work feel like a test she'd fail.
She blames **software firms and government**, not her manager, and wants them taxed.

steps.text: Join the shop and office workers' union this year
Apply for council tenancy officer jobs in the next six months
Stop takeaways and the gym to stretch the two-week cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's terrifying and somebody needs to slow it down. I'd sign every petition going and I'd be at the protest if there was one in town. At work I wouldn't say much, because everyone would be scared and pretending not to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job's gone by 2028, all of it. Maybe I'd still be the one with the keys, walking people round flats, until the robots come in 2031. But I'm not sure they'd even need me for that, because you can already put a code lock on the door and let people look round on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have no idea where to start, that's the truth. I'd go to the union, I'd vote for whoever promised to look after people, and I'd ask Sam if we could move in with his parents to stop paying rent. That's about all I could think of. I can't afford a course and I wouldn't know which course would still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like the floor's gone. Two years is nothing. Two years is two tenancy renewals, and I'd be twenty-nine with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking work goes in 2028 and hands-on work around 2031. What's your job like in those three years in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd be a sort of key-holder, meeting people at doors while a computer did all the talking and the paperwork. It'd be a worse job, less pay, and probably zero-hours. I don't think they'd keep three of us for that, maybe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said move in with Sam's parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, they live in a two-bed with his brother. But Sam's job is caring, and that's hands-on, so maybe he'd have the extra three years and I wouldn't. That's the bit that scares me, that we'd be living on his night shifts with nothing of mine.

say: I'd say it's **terrifying** and must be **slowed down**.
I'd sign petitions and turn up to any **protest** in town.
think: My **desk work** is gone by 2028, and viewings might go to **code locks**.
Between 2028 and 2031 I'd be a **key-holder** on worse pay, if kept at all.
do: Go to the **union** and vote for whoever promises to protect workers.
Ask Sam about moving in with **his parents** to stop paying rent.
Avoid paying for a **course**, since I couldn't tell which would last.
feel: **Panicky**, like the floor has gone, with **no plan** to grab.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. Two years is two tenancy renewals, and I'd be twenty-nine with nothing.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as a downgrade to key-holder, not a safety net.
She'd lean on **Sam's care job**, which is hands-on and buys the household time.
She has **no money** and **no plan**, and says so plainly; panic, not composure.

steps.text: Turn up to union meetings and sign petitions to slow AI down
Vote for the party promising support for laid-off workers
Ask Sam's parents if they could take them in to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, that it needs rules and the people losing out need help. With five years I'd say it louder, because there'd be time to make the government do something. I'd tell the renters' group that if agents go, at least make the landlords register properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is better but I'm not good at using the time. I know myself, I'd tell myself next year and then it's 2030. My desk work goes in 2031, so I'd have maybe three more years of showing flats after that, and I'd be thirty-two by the time that ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get into council housing work in the first couple of years, while they're still hiring people. I'd do the free housing course at the college on Tuesday nights if the union helped. I'd keep going to meetings and maybe stand up and say something, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but it's a slower scared. More like a dentist appointment you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put things off. What would actually make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone I know losing their job. I'm someone who moves when the fire alarm goes, not before. If my colleague Dev got let go, I'd be at the council the next day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam that night, after hearing this card on the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam we can't keep living month to month. Then we'd probably order a pizza anyway, because that's us.

say: I'd say there's **time to make rules** and help people who lose out.
I'd push the renters' group for **landlord registration** if agents disappear.
think: I'd **put things off** until someone near me lost their job.
After my desk work goes in 2031, I'd get **about three years** of showing flats.
do: Apply to **council housing** jobs in the first two years.
Take the **free housing course** on Tuesday nights if the union helps.
Speak up at **union meetings** for the first time.
feel: **Scared**, but slower, like a dentist appointment you know is coming.
S3.quote: I'm someone who moves when the fire alarm goes, not before. If my colleague Dev got let go, I'd be at the council the next day.
fieldNote: She knows her **own pattern**: she waits until the danger is visible.
Five years turns protest into **hoping for rules**, but her own plan stays thin.
Even with time she expects to **lose the job**, so alarm stays, just quieter.

steps.text: Apply for council housing officer roles before 2029
Take the college's free housing course on Tuesday nights
Speak at union meetings about support for agents losing work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to sort out retraining and a safety net, so they'd better. I'd still want unions in every office. I'd post less, because people get bored of you being angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dev got let go, I'd be at the council the next day. That's just as true with ten years. But ten years means I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, maybe with kids by then, and that's worse in a way. Right now I've got nothing to lose, but at thirty-seven with kids I'd have everything to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Barlow & Lane a few more years because the pay is steady and I'm getting better at it. I'd start the housing course in the next year or two and try for a council or housing association job before I'm thirty. Sam and I would probably hold off on kids until one of us had something safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Ten years is a long time. But I know I'd waste some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on kids. Is that a real decision or just a thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real. Sam wants kids sooner than I do anyway. If I knew my job had a sell-by date, I'd want to be somewhere safer first, like a housing association, before we tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your job is talking and paperwork, and how much is being on your feet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two thirds desk, one third out with keys. So the desk part goes in 2036 and the walking part a bit later, if anyone even wants viewings by then. I don't think the extra three years helps me much.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** for real retraining and a **safety net**.
I'd still want a **union** in every office.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd have more to lose than I do now.
My job is **two thirds desk**, so the robot delay barely helps.
do: Stay at Barlow & Lane for a few more years on **steady pay**.
Start the **housing course** and aim for a housing association job before thirty.
Hold off on **having kids** until one of us has a safe job.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, and aware I'd **waste some** of the time.
S4.quote: Right now I've got nothing to lose, but at thirty-seven with kids I'd have everything to lose.
fieldNote: She sees ten years as **riskier** for her life stage, not safer.
The plan to **delay children** is concrete and tied to finding a safe job first.
She knows the **desk share** of her work means the robot delay barely helps.

steps.text: Keep working at Barlow & Lane while learning the lettings side
Enrol on the housing course within two years
Apply to housing associations before turning thirty
Put off trying for children until one job is secure

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years and I've got nothing saved and no other skills. What would help is a proper retraining fund that actually pays your wages while you learn, because I can't do a course and not work. And a union that's already there, not one we have to start in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but if a computer runs lettings, the family in the damp flat has nobody. I'm not a hero, but I do pick up the phone.

headlineQuote: If a computer runs lettings, the family in the damp flat has nobody. I'm not a hero, but I do pick up the phone.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old lettings negotiator** at a small agency in a former mill town.
She earns **low pay**, keeps about **two weeks** of savings, and shares a rented flat with Sam.
She **never uses AI** and keeps a paper diary, and knows she'd be slow to adapt.
She blames **software firms**, and turns to **unions** and votes when worried.
She goes from **uneasy** about rent in the plateau to **panicked** if AGI comes in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she has no savings, no other skills and only two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** that pays wages while she learns.
A **union** already in place before the change, not started in a panic.
